The student council room on the third floor smelled of samosas and marker ink. Pradeep tapped the whiteboard. "So it's settled. Every first-year pays five hundred for the fest, no exceptions. All agreed?"
Eleven hands went up. Siddharth's stayed on the table.
"Half of them pay their own hostel fees," he said. "Making it compulsory isn't fair."
Every face turned. Someone laughed through their nose. Pradeep's smile thinned. "Sid, we need the money. Don't be difficult."
Siddharth felt his neck go warm. Was he being difficult? Everyone here was smart. Maybe he'd missed something in the budget. His phone buzzed: a committee friend had written, "bro why."
He swallowed. "I still think it should be optional. Please put my no in the minutes."
Afterwards, nobody passed him the samosa plate.

qa.q: How much did Pradeep want every first-year to pay?
qa.a: Every first-year was to pay five hundred for the fest, no exceptions.

qa.q: What doubts went through Siddharth's mind when every face turned to him?
qa.a: He wondered whether he really was being difficult and whether he'd missed something in the budget, since everyone else seemed smart.

qa.q: Siddharth asked for his no to go in the minutes. Why was that a meaningful choice?
qa.a: It kept his objection on record calmly, so the fairness question stays visible even though he lost the vote.

qa.q: How might a first-year who pays their own hostel fees see Siddharth's stand if they heard about it?
qa.a: They might feel that at least one council member noticed people like them, and be grateful even though the vote didn't change.

grounding: A young adult who alone disagrees in a council meeting faces stares, pressure and self-doubt, and pays a small social price for holding his view.

It's been a month, and I still remember the heat in my ears. Our sociology group had to run a survey. We got eighty-seven responses. Jatin wanted to write "over two hundred" on the slide. "Nobody checks," he said, and the other three laughed and agreed. I said, "I'm not presenting a number we made up." Four people looked at me like I'd switched off the wifi. For two days the group chat went silent whenever I posted. I lay awake thinking maybe I was being a goody-goody, maybe everyone rounds up. Then the professor asked every group to upload raw data. Jatin messaged me: "ok fine, 87." No thanks, no sorry. Being right didn't feel like winning. It felt like paying a small bill, one I'd pay again.
Amandeep

qa.a: They got eighty-seven responses.

qa.q: What was Amandeep worried about while lying awake after the meeting?
qa.a: Amandeep wondered about being a goody-goody, thinking that maybe everyone rounds up numbers.

qa.q: Looking back, which moment was the real choice, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Saying "I'm not presenting a number we made up" to four laughing teammates was the choice; it cost two days of a silent group chat.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel typing "ok fine, 87"?
qa.a: Jatin may feel embarrassed at being caught by the raw-data rule, which could explain why there is no thanks or sorry.

grounding: A young adult who stands alone against a group's plan to inflate numbers feels stares and doubt, and finds that being right still carries a social cost.

Faculty adviser's note, debating society, 16 September. Written by Vaibhav Sir.

Today's committee meeting voted on whether to disqualify a rival college's speaker for arriving five minutes late to the final. Eleven members voted yes. Yash, twenty, voted no. He said, "The rules say ten minutes, and it was the bus strike. We'd want the same if it were us."

I watched what followed. Several members stared at him; one muttered, "Whose side are you on?" The president asked him twice if he was "sure". Yash's voice stayed level, but his hands were locked together under the table, and he looked at the rulebook, then at me, as if checking he had read it right. After the meeting nobody walked out with him.

What I did next: I checked the rulebook. He was right. I told the committee the speaker stays, and I thanked Yash privately.

qa.q: How many members voted to disqualify the speaker?
qa.a: Eleven members voted yes.

qa.q: What do Yash's locked hands and his glance at the rulebook suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was under strain and doubting himself for a moment, checking he was right even while keeping his voice level.

qa.q: Why did it matter that Vaibhav Sir checked the rulebook and thanked Yash?
qa.a: It confirmed Yash was right and showed him his courage was noticed, which matters when standing alone has cost him socially.

qa.q: How did the other committee members see Yash during the vote?
qa.a: Many saw him as disloyal, asking whose side he was on, and none walked out with him afterwards.

grounding: A young adult who alone disagrees with his committee faces stares, pressure and self-doubt, and his stance costs him socially though he is right.

Tuesday night

All forty of us were supposed to walk out of tomorrow's statistics exam, because the professor added one question from outside the syllabus. The class group had forty thumbs-up. Then it was my turn, and I wrote, "I don't want to walk out. It's one question out of ten. Can we ask for it to be dropped instead?"

The chat went silent for ten minutes. Then: "Rafiq wants marks more than friends." "Traitor." "Enjoy writing alone."

In the canteen people stopped talking when I sat down. I kept thinking, maybe I'm wrong. Maybe I'm just scared. Forty people can't all be wrong.

Disha messaged me privately: "I agree with you. But I can't say it in the group." That helped a little. Also made it lonelier.

I'm still going to write the exam. My hands are cold just thinking about walking in.

qa.q: How many thumbs-up did the walkout plan get in the class group?
qa.a: The class group had forty thumbs-up.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel after the chat went silent and the insults came?
qa.a: Rafiq felt isolated and full of self-doubt, wondering whether this was being right or just being scared, with cold hands at the thought of the exam.

qa.q: What could Disha do that would make Rafiq's stand easier?
qa.a: Disha could say 'I agree' in the group, because one open supporter would make Rafiq far less alone and might free others to speak.

qa.q: Why might Disha agree privately but stay quiet in the group?
qa.a: Disha is likely afraid of being called a traitor too, so the support for Rafiq stays private where the others cannot see.

grounding: A young adult who alone disagrees with the class walkout faces silence, insults and self-doubt, showing the social cost and courage of dissent.

passage: I still remember the project meeting in our final year. Kishore, our group leader, wanted to copy a design from an old senior's thesis and just change the colours. Everyone agreed; there were eight of us, and it was the easy route. When he asked, "Any objections?" I heard myself say, "Yes. I think it's plagiarism." The room went silent. Eight pairs of eyes on me. Someone laughed nervously. Kishore said, "Nobody checks." I felt my stomach flip. For a second I thought, maybe I'm overreacting. After the meeting, two people stopped sitting with me at lunch. For a week I felt like an outsider in my own group. Then the professor announced she'd started checking old theses. Kishore didn't say anything to me, but he redid the design. I'm Lakshmi, and I'd say it again, even with the lonely week.

qa.a: There were eight of us.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel after speaking up?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt the stomach flip of self-doubt, then lonely and like an outsider for a week.

qa.q: Why was Lakshmi's objection worth the cost?
qa.a: It stopped the group from submitting copied work, even though standing alone cost Lakshmi friendship at lunch for a while.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt when the professor announced checks?
qa.a: Kishore likely felt uncomfortable and perhaps embarrassed, realising Lakshmi had been right.

Team coach's note, college debate society, Thursday.
In today's planning meeting, the whole team, eleven members, agreed to argue the "for" side in the national round, because it's easier to prepare. Amandeep alone disagreed. He said the "against" side had stronger evidence and more original arguments. The room went quiet. Tejas, the captain, said, "We've already decided." I watched Amandeep's shoulders go up and his voice get smaller, but he didn't back down: "I just think we'd win more convincingly." Someone rolled their eyes. After the meeting, he sat alone, looking at his notes. I told him that disagreeing with everyone, calmly, took courage, and that I'd ask the team to hear his evidence next week before voting again. He looked relieved, but also tired. Being right doesn't make it easy.

qa.q: How many team members agreed to argue the "for" side?
qa.a: The whole team, eleven members, agreed.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling as his voice got smaller?
qa.a: Amandeep felt pressure and self-doubt, his shoulders rising, yet he held his view.

qa.q: What did the coach do that could help Amandeep?
qa.a: The coach acknowledged his courage and arranged for the team to hear his evidence before voting again.

qa.q: How might Tejas have seen Amandeep's disagreement?
qa.a: Tejas seemed to see it as an obstacle to a decision already made, wanting to move on quickly.

grounding: A young adult who disagrees with his whole debate team feels stares, pressure and self-doubt, and his stance costs something even when he may be right.

Tuesday, 11:30 pm
Hostel meeting tonight. The floor wanted to ban first-years from the common room after 9. Everyone raised their hand. Everyone except me.
I'm Hrithik. I said, "They pay the same fees. That's unfair." The room went dead quiet. Twenty faces turned. Someone laughed. The floor rep said, "Anyone else?" Nobody.
I kept my hand down, but my face was burning. For a second I thought, maybe I'm wrong. Maybe I'm just being difficult.
Now I'm in my room, and Sonali messaged: "You were right, but wow, that was brave." Why didn't she say it in the meeting?
I still think I was right. It just cost more than I expected.

In the village of Kheda, the youth meeting under the peepal tree decided to burn the stubble after harvest, like every year. Charu, back from her agriculture degree, stood up. "The smoke hurts the old people's lungs, and there are machines that can mulch it. The co-operative rents them."
Thirty young men turned to look at her. Somebody snorted. Pranav, her own cousin, muttered, "City ideas."
Charu's knees shook. She wondered for a moment if she'd been away too long to understand. But she didn't sit down. "I'm just saying there's another way."
Walking home, nobody walked with her. Then, at the lane corner, an old woman stopped her. "My chest is bad every November," she said. "Thank you."

qa.q: Where was the youth meeting held?
qa.a: It was held under the peepal tree.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when her knees shook?
qa.a: She felt nervous and self-doubting, wondering if she had been away too long, but determined not to sit down.

qa.q: What could Charu try next to be heard?
qa.a: She could find others who agree, like the old woman, and invite the co-operative to show the machine at the next meeting.

qa.q: How does Pranav see Charu's idea?
qa.a: Pranav dismisses it as "city ideas," seeing her as an outsider rather than listening.

grounding: Shows a young adult standing alone against a village youth meeting, facing stares and self-doubt, and paying a social cost though her view has support.

Dear Nitin bhaiya,
You asked why I sounded low on the phone. Here's the whole thing. Our project group of six voted to skip Professor Rao's extra Saturday lecture as a protest about the deadline. I said I'd still go, because the lecture covers the part of the syllabus I don't understand. You should have seen their faces. One of them said, "So you're choosing marks over us." I went. I sat in the second row almost alone, and I kept thinking everyone was right and I was being selfish. Then the professor explained the exact topic I'd been stuck on for weeks. It helped. But in the group chat, nobody answers me quickly anymore. I know I did the right thing for me. It still costs something.
Jyoti

qa.a: Jyoti felt lonely and doubtful, thinking the group might be right and that going was selfish.

qa.q: What could Jyoti try to repair things with the group?

passage: Hansa, you asked why I skipped the Holi party on our floor. Okay. The week before Holi, someone's earphones went missing, and at the floor meeting everyone decided it must be Shanti didi, the cleaner. Twenty-two people, all nodding. They wanted to complain to the warden and get her moved. And I said, "We have no proof. The earphones could be anywhere." You should have seen the stares. Someone said, "Leela always has to be different." For two days nobody saved me a seat at dinner. I lay awake thinking, maybe I'm naive, maybe everyone sees something I don't. Then on Holi morning the earphones turned up in someone's laundry bag. Nobody apologised to me. Nobody apologised to Shanti didi either. I was right, and it still cost me. I'd do it again, though.
